The prompt and key are accurate. The four options are occupations, and the direct veteran clue makes easy reasonable. Distractor notes match the cited sources.

Michigan Papyrus Collection material supports the papyrus construction note. The alternatives are writing media and easy is reasonable from the Egyptian-logbook context. The scribe, hieroglyph and cross-topic papyrus notes mention papyrus as a medium but none identifies the Merer logbook’s carrier.

Ashmolean catalogue entry AN1910.218 identifies the Linear B tablet as clay and says it details female workers; it also says Evans recognized the subject from pictorial human ideograms before decipherment. The material key, explanation and notes are accurate. Compared with books-publishing-tablet-form, that row asks generally what medium Mesopotamian scribes used for cuneiform; this item tests the substrate of one named Knossos Linear B object. Their broad answer category overlaps, but the artifact, script and source-specific relation differ, so I do not find a duplicate tested fact or direct answer leak. Easy is acceptable for the direct material-identification clue.

The live row equals READY preimage; exact hashes verified. Codex Sinaiticus’s conservation materials identify parchment as prepared animal skin, distinguish hair and flesh sides, and record follicles, veins and scars. The question and explanation are faithful to that examination; the note correctly summarizes preparation. Writing-material alternatives are coherent and easy is defensible because the named surfaces are distinctive. The older Middle Ages card states a general parchment definition but does not identify Codex Sinaiticus’s physical features.
